TITLE: Investigating Transfer Learning for PDEs in Computational Fluid Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Train a Scientific Foundation Model (SFM) on a synthetic dataset of solutions for the 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, using a sequence-to-sequence transformer encoder-decoder architecture, and then fine-tune it on a novel, coupled system such as the 2D Euler equations. Evaluate how well the SFM can generalize knowledge from the unsteady Navier-Stokes training data to the new Euler system.
CONTROLS: Compare with a strong baseline of fine-tuning from scratch on the new Euler system, as well as a version of the SFM model without any pre-training (i.e., from a fixed random initialization).
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (pre-training on the Navier-Stokes dataset: 600 GPU-hours; fine-tuning on the Euler dataset: 400 GPU-hours).
PREDICTION: The SFM should be able to achieve a moderate level of improvement in terms of solution accuracy compared to fine-tuning from scratch, but may fall short of similar results that can be achieved by a fully-trained, monolithic model specific to the Euler equations. This experiment will help determine whether prior knowledge from related PDEs can be transferred effectively to novel systems via a learned surrogate.

TITLE: Physics-Informed Neural Operator Framework for Multi-Physical System Simulation
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural operator framework that can learn to solve multiple physics-based PDEs with different governing equations and boundary conditions, using the same underlying neural network. This framework employs a hierarchical structure where the neural operator first predicts the solution of a reference PDE, and then uses this prediction as input to solve the target PDE.

COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (retraining and validation for different PDEs).
PREDICTION: By reducing the need for retraining and revalidating models on new PDEs, this framework has the potential to provide a unified solution to diverse physics-based modeling problems.

PROPOSAL: Develop a multiscale physics-informed neural network (MS-PINN) that combines the strengths of physics-informed neural networks and multiscale modeling to tackle uncertainty quantification in PDE-constrained optimization problems. TITLE: Large-Scale Physics-Informed Neural Network Optimization for Semi-Supervised Learning of Complex PDEs
PROPOSAL: Develop a large-scale optimization framework for training physics-informed neural networks on semi-supervised learning datasets of complex PDEs. The framework incorporates a combination of batch normalization, adaptive learning rates, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for improved scalability and stability. It also leverages techniques such as knowledge distillation and model ensemble to reduce the number of iterations required for convergence and improve the generalizability of the models.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing large-scale optimization methods for neural networks, such as Adam and SGD with momentum, and study the impact of different data sampling strategies and architectures on the convergence rate and accuracy.
COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours (large-scale optimization and semi-supervised learning experiments).
PREDICTION: By designing a scalable optimization framework for semi-supervised PDE learning, the proposed method can efficiently and accurately learn complex PDE behaviors from large datasets, even with a small number of labeled instances.

Experiments will be conducted using a synthetic dataset of 2D Navier-Stokes equations with varying parameters and geometries.

- A naively initialized model as an ablation.
- A model with manual feature engineering, featuring hand-crafted velocity and pressure terms as inputs.
- A model pre-trained on the same small, diverse set of physical systems as a comparison.
- A model leveraging prior knowledge from domain experts for interpretability.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (data generation and training).
PREDICTION: Initial results will show that having a proper initialization strategy significantly improves learning speed and convergence, while also enhancing interpretability, with potential significant failures in cases where the model is pre-trained on dissimilar systems.
